title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 68 (Power of company to purchase its own securities)

content.overview: Section 68 allows buy-back of own shares or specified securities if articles authorise it and the source, cap, solvency and process conditions are met.
content.glance: Section 68 allows buy-back of own shares or specified securities if articles authorise it and the source, cap, solvency and process conditions are met.
content.study: Buy-back may be financed from free reserves, the securities premium account, or the proceeds of a fresh issue of other shares or specified securities. It cannot be made from the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or securities. The aggregate cap is 25 per cent of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves, and the buy-back of equity shares in a financial year is capped at 25 per cent of paid-up equity capital. A board resolution suffices within the 10 per cent band stated in the section; otherwise a special resolution is required. The debt-equity ratio after buy-back must not exceed 2:1 except for notified classes. Shares must be fully paid. A declaration of solvency is filed. Listed companies also follow SEBI buy-back regulations. Section 70 bars buy-back in the circumstances it names, including default in repayment of deposits, redemption of debentures or preference shares, or payment of dividend, until the default is cured.

examples.title: Same-kind proceeds
examples.body: Buy-back of equity funded by a fresh equity issue is not a permitted source.

examples.title: Default bar
examples.body: An uncured deposit default attracts the s. 70 prohibition.

hypotheticals.facts: Buy-back of equity funded by a fresh equity issue is not a permitted source.

distinctions: Buy-back (ss 68-70) is a purchase. Reduction (s. 66) is a Tribunal-confirmed capital reduction. Treasury-share holding is not the Indian model; bought-back shares are extinguished.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Can a company hold bought-back shares as treasury stock?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: No. The buy-back scheme requires extinguishment and physical destruction or demat equivalent within the prescribed period, not a treasury holding.
